feedback.problem:
A particle moves along a straight line relative to a fixed origin $O$ with acceleration, measured in $\text{m}/{\text{s}}^{2},$ given by the function $a(t)=5-\frac{1}{2}t,$ where $t⩾0$ is the time in seconds. If the particle has velocity $v=3\,\text{m}/\text{s}$ when $t=4\,\text{s},$ calculate the maximum velocity ${v}_{\text{max}}$ of the particle and determine the time when the particle reaches its maximum velocity.

feedback.worked_solution:
The extrema of the velocity $v$ occur at the critical points of $v.$

Since $\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=a(t),$ to find the times where $v$ is a maximum, we just need to solve $a(t)=0$ and test each solution using the first or second derivative test.

Solving $a(t)=0$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}a(t) & =0 \\ 5-\frac{1}{2}t & =0 \\ t & =10.\end{aligned}
$$

So, the extremum of the velocity function occurs when $t=10\,\text{s}.$

We now test the extreme values using the second derivative test. The second derivative is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}v}{\text{d}{t}^{2}} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}) \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(a(t)) \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(5-\frac{1}{2}t) \\  & =-\frac{1}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Since ${v}^{″}(10)<0,$ we conclude that the velocity is maximized when $t=10\,\text{s}.$

Now, we find $v(t)$ by integrating the acceleration with respect to time:

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =\int a(t)\text{d}t \\  & =\int (5-\frac{1}{2}t)\text{d}t \\  & =5t-\frac{1}{4}{t}^{2}+C.\end{aligned}
$$

To determine $C,$ we use the fact that $v(4)=3.$ Substituting this into the above gives

$$
\begin{aligned}5(4)-\frac{1}{4}(4)^{2}+C & =3 \\ 20-4+C & =3\,⟹\,C=-13.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the velocity is given by $v(t)=5t-\frac{1}{4}{t}^{2}-13.$

Finally, we calculate the maximum velocity:

$$
{v}_{\text{max}}=v(10)=5(10)-\frac{1}{4}(10)^{2}-13=12\,\text{m}/\text{s}.
$$

So the maximum velocity ${v}_{\text{max}}=12\,\text{m}/\text{s}$ is reached at $t=10\,\text{s}.$
